Back Extra:

  1. Malignant — a 'bad,' cancerous tumor that invades and spreads; also malignant hypertension, dangerously high BP with organ damage.

Ex: multiparous = giving birth to more than one offspring at a time

  1. Multigravida — a woman who has been pregnant many (more than one) times.

Text: The prefix {{c1::para-}} means {{c2::near, beside, beyond, apart from}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: parasternal = beside the sternum

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Paramedic — literally 'alongside medicine'; the prehospital provider working beside the physician.

  1. Perfusion — blood pouring through the tissues; you judge it (skin color, cap refill, mentation) to catch shock early.

Ex: pericardium = sac around the heart

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT

  1. Polyuria — excessive urination; one of the 'three P's' (with polydipsia and polyphagia) that flags new diabetes/DKA.
  2. Polytrauma — many serious injuries at once; the patient who triggers a full trauma-team activation.
  3. Polypharmacy — many medications taken together; a fall-and-interaction red flag in elderly patients.

Ex: postsurgical = occurring after surgery

Distinguish: opposite is pre- (before)

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Postictal — the drowsy, confused state after a seizure; what you often find on arrival to a seizure call.
  2. Postpartum hemorrhage — bleeding after delivery; a leading cause of maternal death.
  3. Posterior — the 'behind/back' sense; e.g., a posterior wall MI, or auscultating the posterior chest.

Ex: prenatal = occurring before birth

Distinguish: opposite is post- (after)

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Preeclampsia — dangerously high blood pressure in pregnancy that comes before eclampsia's seizures.

Ex: primigravida = pregnant for the first time

Text: The prefix {{c1::pro-}} means {{c2::before, in front of}}.
Back Extra:
WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT

  1. Quadriplegia — paralysis of all four limbs from a high cervical spinal cord injury.

  1. Reflux — acid flowing back up from the stomach (GERD); the burn of heartburn.

Ex: retroperitoneal = area behind the peritoneum

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Retrosternal — behind the sternum; 'retrosternal chest pressure' is the classic charting for cardiac pain.
  2. Retroperitoneal — behind the peritoneum, where the kidneys and aorta lie; a retroperitoneal bleed (ruptured AAA) hides blood in the back.
  3. Retrograde amnesia — loss of memory for events before a head injury (working backward from the impact).

Ex: semiconscious = partially conscious

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Semi-Fowler's — the half-sitting position (about 30–45 degrees) used to ease a patient's breathing.
  2. Semiconscious — only partially awake and responsive; a common way to describe altered mental status.
  3. Semilunar valves — the half-moon-shaped aortic and pulmonic valves of the heart.

Ex: subcutaneous = beneath the skin

Distinguish: opposite is super-/supra- (above)

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT

Text: The prefix {{c1::super-}} means {{c2::above, excessive, or more than normal}}.
Back Extra:
WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT

Ex: suprasternal notch = top of the sternum

  1. Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) — a fast rhythm arising above the ventricles; narrow-complex tach treated with vagal maneuvers or adenosine.

  1. Sympathetic nervous system — nerves acting together for 'fight or flight'; epinephrine is a sympathomimetic that copies it.

Ex: tachycardia = fast heart rate

Ex: tetralogy of Fallot = congenital defect involving four anatomic abnormalities of the heart

Ex: transvaginal = across or through the vagina

Ex: trigeminy = irregular heartbeat of two normal beats followed by one premature beat

Ex: unilateral = one side

Ex: diplopia = double vision

Ex: sextuplets = six offspring of the same pregnancy

Ex: septuplets = seven offspring of the same pregnancy

  3. Amenorrhea — absence of menstrual flow; in a woman of childbearing age, think pregnancy.

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Stethoscope — the instrument you use to auscultate lung and heart sounds and to take a blood pressure.
  2. Laryngoscope — the instrument that lifts the tongue to expose the vocal cords for intubation.
  3. Otoscope — the handheld instrument for looking at the eardrum in a suspected ear infection.

Text: The suffix {{c1::-scopy}} means {{c2::examination with an instrument}}.
Back Extra:
WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Colonoscopy — a scope exam of the colon to screen for polyps and cancer.
  2. Bronchoscopy — threading a scope down the airway to inspect the bronchi or retrieve an inhaled foreign body.
  3. Arthroscopy — inserting a camera into a joint (like the knee) to diagnose and repair it.

Text: The suffix {{c1::-sis}} means {{c2::a process, action, or condition}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: see also -osis.

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Diagnosis — the process of working out which disease is producing the patient's signs and symptoms.
  2. Prognosis — the predicted course and outcome of a disease (what happens next).
  3. Sepsis — the whole-body condition of a dysregulated, life-threatening response to infection.

Text: The suffix {{c1::-stasis}} means {{c2::stopping or controlling flow}}.
Back Extra:
Meaning: slowing or stopping the normal flow of a fluid, such as blood (eg, hemostasis).

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Hemostasis — the stopping of blood flow; what direct pressure or a tourniquet achieves on a bleed.
  2. Cholestasis — stoppage of bile flow that backs up and yellows the skin (jaundice).
  3. Homeostasis — the body holding its internal conditions (temperature, blood sugar, pH) in a steady, controlled balance.

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Chemotaxis — the ordered movement of white blood cells toward chemical signals at a site of infection.
  2. Phototaxis — the directed movement of a cell or organism toward or away from light.
  3. Thermotaxis — the directed movement of cells or organisms along a temperature gradient.

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Hypertrophic — as in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: overgrown heart muscle; a hidden cause of sudden cardiac arrest in young athletes.
  2. Atrophic — atrophic (wasted) muscle in a limb long immobilized in a cast or paralyzed after a stroke.
  3. Dystrophic — faulty tissue nourishment or development, as in muscular dystrophy or dystrophic calcification of damaged tissue.

Ex: cardiology = the study of the heart

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Cardiology — the study and medicine of the heart (the cardiologist who catheterizes your STEMI patient).
  2. Neurology — the study of the nervous system: strokes, seizures, and neuropathies.
  3. Toxicology — the study of poisons and overdoses; the field behind the "tox screen" and Poison Control.

Ex: pulmonologist = specialist in diseases of the lung

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Radiologist — the specialist who reads your patient's X-rays, CT, and MRI.
  2. Nephrologist — the kidney specialist who manages dialysis patients.
  3. Oncologist — the cancer specialist who directs chemotherapy.

Text: The directional term {{c1::anterior (ventral)}} means {{c2::toward the front surface of the body}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: opposite is posterior (dorsal)

WHERE YOU'LL USE IT
  1. Anterior STEMI — ST elevation in V1–V4; the front wall of the heart (left ventricle) is infarcting.
  2. Anterior shoulder dislocation — the most common type (~95%); the humeral head slips forward off the socket.
  3. Ventral hernia — a bulge pushing through the anterior (ventral) abdominal wall, seen on the front of the belly.

Text: The directional term {{c1::posterior (dorsal)}} means {{c2::toward the back surface of the body}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: opposite is anterior (ventral)

WHERE YOU'LL USE IT
  1. Log roll — rolling the trauma patient to inspect and palpate the posterior chest and spine for hidden wounds.
  2. Prone position — the patient lies face-down, so the posterior (dorsal) surface of the body faces up; supine is the opposite.
  3. Posterior STEMI — ST depression in V1–V3 with tall R waves; confirm it with posterior leads V7–V9.

Text: The directional term {{c1::superior}} means {{c2::closest to the head}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: opposite is inferior

WHERE YOU'LL USE IT
  1. Superior vena cava (SVC) — drains blood from everything above the heart: the head, neck, and arms.
  2. Fowler's position — sitting the patient up by raising the superior (head) end of the stretcher to ease breathing.
  3. Charting: "Laceration 3 cm superior to the right eyebrow."

Text: The directional term {{c1::inferior}} means {{c2::closest to the feet}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: opposite is superior

WHERE YOU'LL USE IT
  1. Inferior STEMI — ST elevation in II, III, and aVF; the bottom wall of the heart, classically the right coronary artery.
  2. Inferior vena cava (IVC) — the large vein returning blood from everything below the heart: legs, pelvis, and abdomen.
  3. Charting: "Obvious deformity to the leg just inferior to the right knee."

Text: The directional term {{c1::proximal}} means {{c2::closest to the point of attachment}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: opposite is distal

WHERE YOU'LL USE IT
  1. Tourniquet placement — goes 2–3 inches proximal to the wound (between the bleed and the trunk) to stop arterial flow.
  2. Proximal humerus fracture — a break near the shoulder end of the arm bone; classic after an elderly fall.
  3. Charting: "Traumatic amputation of the left leg proximal to the knee."

Text: The directional term {{c1::distal}} means {{c2::farthest from the point of attachment}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: opposite is proximal

WHERE YOU'LL USE IT
  1. Distal PMS check — after splinting, you reassess pulse, motor, and sensation distal to the injury to confirm circulation.
  2. Distal radius fracture — the classic Colles' fracture at the wrist end of the forearm after a fall on an outstretched hand.
  3. Capillary refill — pressed at the most distal point, the fingertip or nailbed; sluggish return signals poor perfusion.

Text: The directional term {{c1::medial}} means {{c2::closest to the midline}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: opposite is lateral

WHERE YOU'LL USE IT
  1. Medial malleolus — the bony knob on the inner ankle (end of the tibia); tenderness here triggers the Ottawa ankle rules.
  2. MCL sprain — the medial collateral ligament on the inner knee, torn by a blow to the outer knee.
  3. Charting: "Laceration to the medial aspect of the left thigh, near the groin."

Text: The directional term {{c1::lateral}} means {{c2::farthest from the midline}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: opposite is medial

WHERE YOU'LL USE IT
  1. Lateral malleolus — the bump on the outer ankle (end of the fibula); the most common spot for sprain tenderness.
  2. Left lateral recumbent (recovery) position — rolling an unresponsive, breathing patient onto their side to protect the airway.
  3. Lateral STEMI — ST elevation in I, aVL, V5, and V6; the side wall of the left ventricle.

Text: The directional term {{c1::deep}} means {{c2::farthest from the surface of the skin}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: opposite is superficial

WHERE YOU'LL USE IT
  1. Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) — a clot in the deep leg veins (not the surface ones); can break loose and cause a PE.
  2. Deep tendon reflexes (DTRs) — tapping the patellar tendon beneath the skin to test the reflex arc.
  3. Charting: "Deep laceration to the forearm exposing muscle and fat."

Text: The directional term {{c1::superficial}} means {{c2::closest to the surface of the skin}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: opposite is deep

WHERE YOU'LL USE IT
  1. Superficial (first-degree) burn — involves only the outer skin layer; red and painful like a sunburn, no blisters.
  2. Superficial veins — the surface arm veins just under the skin that you target when starting an IV.
  3. Charting: "Superficial abrasion to the knee, no deep tissue involved."
